hero.name: Usha
hero.who: a 64-year-old retired postmistress in Bhubaneswar who is sure she reads people well

story.b: Usha spent thirty-five years behind the counter of a post office in Bhubaneswar, and she has always believed she can read anyone in a minute. Since retiring, she rents out the room above her house in Saheed Nagar. Last year she chose a smart, smiling young man who spoke politely and touched her feet. He left in March owing three months of rent. Before him, she had turned away a shy engineering student because he would not look her in the eye. She later heard from her neighbour that he was the most honest boy in his hostel. Now the room is empty again. Usha sits on her verandah with her tea, unsure of her own judgment for the first time.

ask.q: Usha trusted a charming tenant who cheated her and rejected a shy honest one. What should she question first?
o: Whether she can really judge strangers from how they seem in a few minutes
Whether she should ever rent to young people again
Whether her neighbour gave her the wrong information
ask.why: Both mistakes came from the same habit: judging strangers by charm or shyness in a short meeting. Banning young tenants turns two bad experiences into a blanket rule, and blaming the neighbour avoids the real lesson about how hard it is to read strangers.

chapters.take: Feeling sure about a stranger is not the same as understanding them.

story.b: One morning Usha's phone rings while she is chopping beans. A polite young man says he is calling from the pension office. Her life certificate has a problem, he explains, and her pension will stop next month unless she confirms an OTP he is about to send. He knows her name and her old post office. He sounds kind and worried for her. Usha's fingers are already reaching for the message. Then she stops. She has spent her life assuming people tell the truth, and mostly that has served her well. But this is money, and the call came out of nowhere. She tells him she will call back, and he suddenly sounds impatient.

ask.q: A kind-sounding caller asks Usha for an OTP to save her pension. What should she do?
o: Share it, since he knew her name and seemed genuine
Ask him a few personal questions to test if he is real
Hang up and contact the pension office through its official number or in person
ask.why: Most of us start by believing people, which is why polite callers can fool even careful people. Knowing her name proves nothing, and quizzing him still keeps her inside his story. Hanging up and using an official contact checks the truth without relying on his words.

chapters.take: We naturally assume honesty. For money or details, verify before you act.

story.b: Two people come to see the room on the same Sunday. The first is a cheerful man in a pressed shirt who praises her garden and laughs easily. The second is a young lab technician named Mitali, who fidgets, speaks softly and keeps checking her phone. Usha's gut instantly prefers the cheerful man. Then she remembers last year. This time she asks both for the same things: a work ID, a past landlord's number and a month's deposit. Mitali brings everything the next day and explains she was nervous because she was waiting for her mother's test results. The cheerful man never sends his landlord's number, and soon stops answering her calls.

ask.q: One applicant is charming and calm, the other nervous. How should Usha decide?
o: Pick the charming one, since calm people are usually honest
Check both through their actions, like documents and past landlords
Pick the nervous one, since nervous people cannot lie well
ask.why: Faces and manners are a poor guide to honesty. Some honest people look nervous and some dishonest people look perfectly relaxed. Checking what each person actually does gives far better information than either the charming smile or the shaky voice.

chapters.take: Judge strangers by what they do, not by how they look while doing it.

story.b: A month after moving in, Mitali comes home late and sits with Usha for dinner. She mentions, almost laughing, that her mother's condition back in Cuttack has got worse and she may need surgery. Then she jokes about the hospital canteen food. Usha's neighbour Bina, who is visiting, raises her eyebrows. Later at the gate, Bina whispers that the girl does not seem to care much about her own mother. Usha almost agrees. But she remembers how calm and smiling the cheating tenant had been. Faces do not always match feelings. The next morning she leaves a tiffin of dalma outside Mitali's door and asks, gently, how she is really coping.

ask.q: Mitali jokes while sharing bad news about her mother. Bina calls her uncaring. What should Usha do?
o: Give her the benefit of the doubt and gently ask how she is coping
Agree with Bina, since the laughter shows how she truly feels
Stay out of it, since a tenant's family is not her business
ask.why: People often show feelings in ways that do not match what is inside, and nervous laughter can hide deep worry. Calling her uncaring would be unfair, and staying completely out of it leaves a frightened young woman alone. A gentle question and a little support open the door.

chapters.take: When someone reacts strangely, their outside may not match their inside. Ask before judging.

story.h: The dark corner by the park
story.b: Every evening, the corner behind the colony park turns noisy. The streetlight there has been broken for months, and young men race their bikes through the narrow lane after dark. Twice, elderly walkers have nearly been hit. At the residents' meeting, people blame the boys of today and talk about calling their parents. Usha has a different thought. The racing happens only on that one dark, empty stretch, never on the bright main road. Maybe the place matters as much as the people. She offers to write to the municipal office about the light and asks for a speed breaker. Three weeks later, the light is fixed and the breaker is painted yellow. The racing almost stops.

ask.q: Young men race bikes only on one dark stretch of lane. What will most likely reduce it?
o: Blame the boys' upbringing and complain to their parents
Change the place itself, with a working light and a speed breaker
Ignore it, since such boys will race somewhere anyway
ask.why: Behaviour is often tied to particular places and conditions. Remove the dark, empty stretch, and the risky behaviour often drops sharply. Blaming character changes nothing about the lane, and assuming they will simply race elsewhere ignores how much the setting invites it.

chapters.take: Behaviour often lives in a place. Change the place and the behaviour can change.

story.b: A new neighbour, Mr Panda, moves into the house opposite. He is about Usha's age, tall and serious. Every morning Usha waves to him from her verandah, and every morning he walks past without a word. Within a week the colony has decided he is proud and rude. Usha feels the same irritation rising. Then she reminds herself how often this year her quick judgments have been wrong. She decides to hold her opinion loosely. One evening she walks over with a plate of pithas sent by Mitali's mother, who is now recovering well. Up close, Mr Panda smiles warmly. He explains that he lost most of his hearing years ago and often misses greetings from far away.

ask.q: The colony says the new neighbour is rude because he ignores greetings. What should Usha do?
o: Agree with the colony and stop greeting him
Ask other neighbours more about him before deciding
Hold her first impression loosely and get to know him directly
ask.why: Understanding strangers is hard, and first impressions are often wrong. Holding her judgment loosely and meeting him herself gives her a real chance to learn the truth. Following the colony's verdict spreads an unfair label, and asking around mostly collects the same guesses.

chapters.take: Approach strangers with humility. Your first impression is a guess, not a fact.

story.b: By winter, Usha's verandah is busier than it has been in years. Mitali still rents the room upstairs and has become almost family. Her mother came to stay for a week after the surgery and taught Usha a new way to make chhena poda. Mr Panda joins them for tea on Sundays, sitting close so he can hear. The lane behind the park is quiet in the evenings. When an unknown number calls about a prize she never entered, Usha simply hangs up. She still trusts people, and she still likes them. But she no longer trusts her first glance so completely. Now she watches what people do, asks gentle questions and stays open to being wrong.

chapters.take: Trust people, but hold quick judgments lightly. Strangers are rarely what they first seem.
